planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped stock in fall or early spring into deep, well-drained soil in a permanent site, since beech resents transplanting once established and roots stay shallow.

directions: Choose a permanent, deep, well-drained site in full sun to light shade before planting, since this grafted selection shares the shallow, disturbance-sensitive root system of European beech. Dawyck Purple is a narrow, strongly fastigiate sport of the purple beech line, selected at the Dawyck estate in Scotland, holding a tight columnar silhouette with deep purple-maroon foliage that is noticeably narrower than seedling purple beeches. Its upright form makes it useful where a shade tree's bold color is wanted but horizontal space is limited, such as along drives or as a vertical accent among lower plantings. Growth is slow to moderate, and the tree needs a genuine winter chill to perform and color well, struggling in hot, humid climates.

planting.note: Plant container or balled-and-burlapped trees in fall or early spring in deep, well-drained soil, siting them permanently since beech dislikes root disturbance.

directions: Site this old European cultivar in deep, well-drained soil with room for a dense, rounded crown, in full sun to partial shade. Fernleaf Beech bears narrow, deeply and irregularly cut leaves, some nearly threadlike, giving the whole canopy an unusually fine, lacy texture that distinguishes it sharply from typical beech foliage, with leaf shape varying considerably even on the same branch. It forms a handsome, dense specimen tree with smooth gray bark that remains ornamental through winter once leaves drop. Like other European beech selections it is slow-growing and long-lived, performs best with a real winter chill, and should not be planted where summers are consistently hot and humid.

planting.note: Plant container-grown trees in spring in deep, well-drained soil; as a dioecious species, a male pollinator tree is needed nearby for the female trees to set nuts.

directions: Grow Chinese torreya in deep, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade, allowing room for a slow-growing, pyramidal to broadly conical evergreen conifer. This yew relative has been cultivated for over a thousand years in Zhejiang Province, China, chiefly for its olive-sized seeds, which are roasted and eaten as a snack nut or pressed for a culinary oil once the fleshy outer coat is removed. Trees are dioecious, so both a male and female tree are required for nut production, and seedlings are notably slow to begin bearing, often taking a decade or more. The stiff, flattened needles are sharp-tipped and spirally arranged, giving the tree a somewhat yew- or fir-like appearance year-round, and mature specimens tolerate some shade better than many other coniferous nut trees.
sources: Journal of Economic Botany (Torreya grandis nut production literature)

planting.note: Plant grafted standards in spring in well-drained, adaptable soil in full sun; stake the young top-grafted head until the trunk has established enough strength to support the weeping canopy.

directions: Plant this top-grafted selection in well-drained, urban-tolerant soil in full sun, giving the cascading canopy open room to develop its picturesque form. Weeping Japanese Pagoda Tree produces long, pendulous, contorted branches that drape to the ground from a grafted head, creating a dense green mound or, when trained upward on a trunk, an umbrella-like specimen prized mainly for winter silhouette and summer shade rather than for flowers, since grafted weeping forms bloom sparingly if at all. It shares the species' exceptional tolerance of heat, drought, compacted soil, and air pollution, making it a durable choice for small urban and courtyard gardens where a conventional shade tree would outgrow the space. Little pruning is needed beyond removing any upright reversion shoots that arise below the graft union.

planting.note: Plant container or bare-root trees in spring in well-drained soil; tolerant of wind, salt spray, heat, and urban conditions once roots are established.

directions: Plant Chinese hackberry in well-drained soil in full sun, allowing a broad, rounded canopy of glossy, leathery, evergreen-to-semi-evergreen leaves to develop; in colder parts of its range it drops leaves briefly in winter. Small orange to reddish-brown drupes ripen in autumn and are relished by birds, while the smooth, often warty gray bark and twiggy, somewhat zigzag branching give the tree interest through the dormant season. Widely planted as a street and park tree across southern China, Japan, and Taiwan, and increasingly used in bonsai for its small leaves and fine ramification, it tolerates heat, wind, coastal salt, and compacted urban soils with ease. It is notably more cold-tender than the familiar American hackberry, so it should be reserved for warm-temperate and subtropical gardens.

planting.note: Plant container-grown stock in spring in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in full sun to partial shade; still uncommon in trade, so source from specialty woody-plant nurseries.

directions: Site Chinese Parrotia in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil with protection from the hottest afternoon sun, since it is adapted to the sheltered ravine forests of eastern China where it survives as a rare, scattered relict population. Close kin to the better-known Persian ironwood, it differs in its more rounded leaf base and a generally more upright, multi-stemmed habit, and it shares that relative's smooth, flaking, patchwork bark that colors attractively with age. Fall display is a strong draw, with leaves turning shades of yellow, orange, and red, often with several colors present on the plant at once. Though critically rare in the wild, it has been propagated and distributed by specialty arboreta and nurseries in recent decades as a garden-worthy alternative or companion to Parrotia persica.
